description: I am George, a rotating equipment engineer in the oil and gas industry, based in Bintulu, with experience in turbomachinery condition data. I build data tools and dashboards in Python and JavaScript, and use AI to turn large sets of technical reports into findings that can be traced to the source. I like building systems that let the data speak for itself. Entering solo, open to one teammate for video or design.
summary:
Flame in Freefall turns NASA's PSI microgravity combustion data into fire-safety answers for crewed habitats. We merged the test tables of all 24 PSI combustion investigations into one table of 2,009 tests, each linked to its source file and row. The dashboard ranks the investigations for five habitats (ISS, Gateway, Moon base, pressurized rover, Mars base) with a re-weightable score and plans 9 tests that would close every habitat gap. The key finding: no solid material in PSI was tested above 22.2% oxygen, while a Moon base is planned at about 34%. Drag any cabin's oxygen and pressure and the dashboard counts the NASA tests in that air, names the closest one, and runs a droplet-flame model tested on held-out test days, which predicts for ISS air and refuses Moon air. A lunar gravity check sets NASA Glenn's 2025 allowance of up to 2.3 oxygen points beside drop tests that measured up to 5.6 for Mylar. An SI assistant answers only from NASA documents, cites the supporting sentence, and shows how many of its numbers match the data. Quotes are machine-checked, and the table passes 1,012 of 1,012 audit checks against the original NASA files.

Live app: https://flame-in-freefall-three.vercel.app
details:
Live app: https://flame-in-freefall-three.vercel.app

WHAT IT DOES

Flame in Freefall is a web dashboard over NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion data. It answers each line of the challenge:

- Summarizes: a page for each of the 24 PSI combustion investigations with its objective, fuels, tested conditions, publications, NASA flame photos, and key findings quoted word for word from NASA reports.

- Ranks: pick ISS, Gateway, Moon base, pressurized rover or Mars base, and the investigations are ranked by topic and by how close their tests come to that habitat's oxygen, pressure and airflow. The score is visible and every weight can be changed.

- Interprets: no solid material in PSI was tested above 22.2% oxygen, while a lunar habitat is planned at 33.5 to 35% (NASA/TM-2013-217377). Nine newer Saffire IV-VI flight tests that are not in PSI yet are included as sourced rows; six burned solids between 25.4% and 31.0% oxygen.

- Check any cabin air: drag oxygen and pressure, or pick a habitat. The card counts the NASA tests in that air, names the closest test with its source row, runs the droplet-flame model or refuses with the distance, and adds the lunar gravity evidence. Every state has its own link.

- Predicts, within limits: a model of whether a FLEX droplet flame goes out on its own, tested on held-out test days (AUC 0.85, Brier skill +0.35, 273 tests). It predicts for ISS air (heptane 34%, 95% range 21-47%) and refuses Moon air, which is 0.14 atm below the lowest FLEX test.

- Gravity: NASA Glenn's 2025 allowance for six materials is up to 2.3 oxygen points; drop-tower tests measured up to 5.6 for Mylar (Olson and Ferkul 2012). 24 measured lunar and Martian gravity points from 7 NASA sources are charted. No measured test reaches 34% oxygen at 8.2 psia in lunar gravity.

- Plans tests: "Fly these tests first" picks the fewest test conditions that close every habitat gap: 9 tests close 15 of 15. One solid-material test at 33.5-35% oxygen and 8.1-8.3 psia covers the Moon base, Mars base and rover at once. Downloadable as a CSV test matrix.

- For PSI curators: 65 rows flagged by fixed rules for review (repeated rows, text in number columns, oxygen on the wrong scale, negative airflow, an impossible pressure), each linked to its file and row. Flagged, not confirmed errors.

- Ask the data: an assistant beside every page answers only from the PSI and NASA documents, cites the supporting sentence, shows how many of its numbers match the data, and says when the documents do not cover a question.

- Equipment and Earth: investigations grouped by prevention, detection and suppression, and Earth uses quoted from NASA Spinoff.

- 3D evidence space: oxygen x pressure x gravity in one rotating view; Moon base air sits alone at lunar gravity with no NASA test beside it. Plan NASA's next flights: pick flights and see how many habitat gaps close.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline merges the 22 PSI experimental tables into one 2,009-row table, keeping the source file and row for every value. Habitat atmospheres come from cited NASA reports; where NASA gives no value it is shown as not specified and left out of the scoring. Code re-checks the table against the original PSI files (1,012 of 1,012 checks pass) and checks 259 quotes word for word against saved NASA source text (key findings, Earth uses, lunar gravity, Saffire IV-VI, partial gravity). The data-health scan also found a sign error in our own parser (8 negative airflows read as positive); it is fixed and covered by a test. The Ask assistant was scored on 100 questions whose checks were written before the run: 94 passed, all 25 trap questions were refused, and 98.2% of the numbers in answers matched the data. The site is static HTML and JavaScript with Plotly, hosted on Vercel; Ask is a Python function calling Claude with NASA documents, six data tools and citations.

WHY IT MATTERS

Exploration habitats will run at higher oxygen and lower pressure than the ISS, where materials burn more readily, and at partial gravity. The dashboard shows where NASA's fire data stops, ranks what is most useful for each habitat, plans the fewest tests that would close the gaps, and gives PSI curators a list of rows to review. It never interpolates beyond the tested range: the model refuses outside its data, and partial-gravity values are shown only as measured.

TOOLS

Python 3.12 (numpy, scipy), JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Plotly.js, Vercel, NASA PSI and NTRS, Claude (Anthropic).

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

SI (Claude, Anthropic) was used to help research the challenge and sources, write and test code, extract candidate quotes and values from NASA reports, and draft text. The project direction was set by the team. Every quoted value is machine-checked word for word against its NASA source, all data processing is plain code with automated tests, and the Ask panel is an SI model restricted to the loaded NASA documents. The demo video's narration voice (Microsoft Edge neural TTS) and music (ACE-Step 1.5) are AI-generated and labelled on screen. No AI-generated images or video are used; flame footage is real NASA BASS-II flight video.
